items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: I would become friends with Yusef Lateef, with Elvin Jones, with Paul Chambers, people like that that would be there occasionally.

ctx.x: Yeah. Can you describe for us what that was like? What would the tunes be? And was the function of it partly to meet people, to maybe find gigs and just improve yourself?

No. The function of it, mind you I’m the young guy. I’m just there you know. I’m out of the exterior if you will. The function of it was to touch base. The musicians that would gather there each and every Sunday that might be in town or might be at home, but just meet and have a good time playing music. So what? It wasn’t about having a gig or anything like that. Because as I mentioned before on the way to New York, now that I’m out of the Army where I practiced my bass every night until three or four in the…
Did you join the military or were you drafted?

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: until a gig came, a concert came with — who was I with, that was with Yusef Lateef.

ctx.x: Well that sort of addressed a question I had in mind because I was reading through your discography and the list of all the people that you’ve played with and who have played with you as a leader, and I’m curious why you were chosen so often, why were you the bass player of choice so many hundreds of times?

Well let me put it this way: I’m my worst, I’ve been over the years, my worst critic. It continued. Until recently I never could appreciate what I’ve done. There’s always more and more that I could learn. And I don’t see that romantically, that’s realistic, you know, reality and so forth. But last summer my wife, knowing that I would return from the Conservatory at Boston at about 7:00, when I walked in there was this record going. And I said, “Wow, who is the bass player? If I could play like that, that’s where…
Nice. Well speaking of recognizing yourself and going back in your career, I came across an article that a critic, you performed at the Carnegie Hall in 1984 with Chico Freeman, just a duet.
